parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by a photon.
hints: Hint 1: Think about how light energy is delivered - is it continuous like a flowing stream, or does it arrive in tiny discrete packets?
Hint 2: Recall what type of radiation these packets belong to, and link the word quantum to a discrete amount of energy.
parts.proper_answer: A photon is a discrete quantum (packet) of energy of electromagnetic radiation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Light Is Made Of**
Think of electromagnetic radiation not as a smooth continuous wave for energy transfer, but as arriving in tiny indivisible lumps. Each lump is called a photon. A common mistake is to call it a particle like an electron - it has no mass or charge, it is purely an energy packet.

Step 2: **Complete Definition**
So you need both ideas for full marks: it is a quantum meaning a discrete packet, and it is of electromagnetic radiation. Its energy is given by $$E = hf$$ where $h$ is the Planck constant and $f$ is frequency.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
Electromagnetic radiation of a varying frequency $f$ and constant intensity $I$ is used to illuminate a metal surface. At certain frequencies, electrons are emitted from the surface of the metal. The variation with $f$ of the maximum kinetic energy $E_{\text{MAX}}$ of the emitted electrons is shown in Fig. 7.1.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State the name of this phenomenon.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on what is happening physically - light shines on a metal and electrons escape from the surface. What is the standard name for light-induced electron emission?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognising the Process**
You shine electromagnetic radiation onto a metal surface and electrons are ejected from the surface. This one-to-one interaction where a photon gives its energy to a surface electron to release it is called the photoelectric effect.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Describe **three** conclusions that can be drawn from the graph in Fig. 7.1. The conclusions may be qualitative or quantitative.

markscheme_points.text: there is a frequency below which no electrons are emitted or threshold frequency = 5.4 × 10^14 Hz
markscheme_points.guidance: Any three bullet points, 1 mark each

markscheme_points.text: work function of the metal = 3.6 × 10^-19 J (or 2.2 eV)
markscheme_points.guidance: Any three bullet points, 1 mark each
Any three bullet points, 1 mark each

markscheme_points.text: gradient of the line is the Planck constant or gradient of the line is 6.7 × 10^-34 J s
markscheme_points.guidance: Any three bullet points, 1 mark each

hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at where the line meets the frequency axis - what does it tell you about low frequencies where $E_{MAX}$ is zero?
Hint 2: Think about how the photoelectric equation $E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$ matches the form $y = mx + c$ for this straight-line graph.
Hint 3: Consider what the x-intercept, the extrapolated y-intercept, and the slope of the line each represent physically, and estimate values from the grid.
parts.proper_answer: Any three from: Threshold frequency $f_0 = 5.4 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}$ below which no electrons emitted. Work function $\Phi = hf_0 = 3.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$ (2.2 eV). $E_{MAX}$ increases linearly with $f$ above threshold. Gradient $= h = 6.7 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$ (Planck constant).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Threshold Frequency From the Intercept**
The line does not start at the origin. It cuts the $f$-axis at about $5.4 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}$. Below this frequency $E_{MAX}$ is zero, so no electrons are emitted. This is the threshold frequency $f_0$.

Step 2: **Work Function From Energy Conservation**
Use $$E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$$ where $\Phi$ is the work function. At threshold, $E_{MAX}=0$, so $$\Phi = hf_0$$ Reading $f_0 = 5.4 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}$ gives $$\Phi \approx 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 5.4 \times 10^{14} \approx 3.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$$ This is the minimum energy needed to escape the metal.

Step 3: **Linear Rise and Gradient is h**
Above $f_0$, $E_{MAX}$ rises linearly with $f$. Comparing $$E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$$ with $y = mx + c$, the gradient $m = h$, the Planck constant. From the graph, e.g. rise $\approx 3.0 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$ for run $\approx 4.5 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}$ gives $$h \approx 6.7 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem:
The experiment in **(b)** is repeated twice, each time making one change.

State, with a reason, how the graph obtained would compare with Fig. 7.1 when:

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: a different metal is used, but keeping the intensity $I$ of the radiation the same

markscheme_points.text: (line has) same gradient but different intercept

hints: Hint 1: Ask yourself which quantity in $E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$ is a property of the metal itself and which is a universal constant.
Hint 2: Think about how a change in that metal property shifts the intercepts but leaves the slope of the $E_{MAX}$ against $f$ line unchanged.
parts.proper_answer: Different threshold frequency (different x-intercept) because different metal has different work function. Same gradient $h$ as Planck constant is universal, so line is parallel but shifted.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why the Intercept Moves**
A different metal means electrons are bound by a different amount, so the work function $\Phi$ is different. Since $$hf_0 = \Phi$$ the threshold frequency $f_0$ must be different, so the x-intercept changes.

Step 2: **Why the Gradient Stays the Same**
From $$E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$$ the gradient is $h$, the Planck constant. This is a fundamental constant of nature, not a property of the metal. So the new line has the same gradient but a different intercept - it is parallel to Fig. 7.1.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: the same metal is used, but with electromagnetic radiation of intensity $2I$.
hints: Hint 1: Remember what intensity means in the photon picture - does doubling intensity change the energy of each photon or just the number arriving per second?
Hint 2: Check the photoelectric equation to see if intensity appears in the expression for maximum kinetic energy of a single emitted electron.
parts.proper_answer: Graph is unchanged (same line). Photons still have same energy $hf$ as frequency is unchanged; higher intensity only increases number of photons and hence number of electrons, not $E_{MAX}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Intensity Changes Number, Not Energy**
Intensity is power per unit area. In photons, doubling intensity at the same frequency means twice as many photons per second, but each photon still has energy $$E = hf$$ unchanged.

Step 2: **No Change to E_MAX**
Since $$E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$$ depends only on $f$ and $\Phi$, and neither has changed, $E_{MAX}$ at each frequency is identical. The line is exactly the same. Only the rate of emission (photoelectric current) doubles.
